narrative:
The model predicts an 11% chance that you will fail your final year, which is low but enough for the school to require you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The three factors that most influenced this decision were your number of past failures, your desire to pursue higher education, and the amount of time you spend studying each week. Past failures had the strongest effect. Even though you have had zero failed classes—matching the average for students who passed—this absence of prior setbacks still pushed the prediction slightly toward failing in the model’s logic. Your strong ambition to continue into higher education worked in your favor and pulled the prediction back toward passing. However, your limited weekly study time of less than two hours worked against you; most students who passed dedicate two to five hours, so your shorter sessions increased the chance the model saw you failing.

Because the overall risk is modest, the school is simply being cautious. To improve, focus on increasing your study time to at least two hours most days. Building consistent study habits now will strengthen your performance and reduce any future need for extra courses.
